D7: Developer Productivity & Operational Enablement

How to read this diagram
  1. Start at Rung 1: the whole idea in one paragraph. Read this first.
  2. Move to Rung 2 only if you need mechanisms: orders of operation and failure modes.
  3. Climb to Rung 3 for worked examples with numbers, scenario shapes, and exam traps.

What breaks if a part fails: if you skip Rung 1, you will drown in detail before you know what the chapter is about.

You are the architect who rolls out Claude-powered tools to a whole engineering org and keeps them running. Three jobs. First: configure tools like Claude Code so 200 developers get the same safe, consistent setup. Second: design AI-assisted workflows that speed developers up without letting bad code ship faster. Third: debug production Claude systems and write the runbooks the on-call team follows at 3am. The exam tests design decisions and trade-offs here, not memorized config flags.

What this domain is really about

You are the architect who rolls out Claude-powered tools to a whole engineering org and keeps them running. Three jobs:

  1. Configure tools like Claude Code so 200 developers get the same safe, consistent setup.
  2. Design AI-assisted workflows that speed developers up without letting bad code ship faster.
  3. Debug production Claude systems and write the runbooks the on-call team follows at 3am.

The exam tests design decisions and trade-offs here, not memorized config flags.

Three official objectives, and this volume covers each one fully:

  1. Configure Claude tools and environments for teams (for example, Claude Code).
  2. Improve developer workflows using AI-assisted tooling.
  3. Support debugging and operational issue resolution.

1. The developer-productivity problem: what slows a team down

How to read this diagram
  1. Read the three red/amber/purple panels: each names one drag and its symptom.
  2. Drift: every machine behaves differently, so debugging becomes guesswork.
  3. Unsafe speed: AI writes faster than reviewers read, so defects ship at machine speed.
  4. Invisible failures: production LLM systems fail where no debugger looks.
  5. Read the bottom row: the stack fixes all three, bottom to top. Each layer assumes the one below it.

What breaks if a part fails: if environments drift, the same prompt produces different code and every layer above rests on sand.

Rung 1: the one-paragraph version. One developer with an AI coding tool is a personal preference: fast loops, own rules, own risk. Two hundred developers with AI coding tools is an operations problem. Three things slow the org down:

  1. Drift: every machine behaves differently, so the same prompt produces different code and debugging becomes guesswork.
  2. Unsafe speed: AI writes code faster than reviewers can read it, so defects ship at machine speed unless gates catch them.
  3. Invisible failures: production LLM systems fail in ways no debugger shows, so without traces and runbooks the on-call team is blind.

This volume climbs the stack that fixes all three, bottom to top: consistent environments, guardrailed tools, gated workflows with guarded data, debuggable systems, and runbooks. Each layer assumes the one below it.

Rung 2: one level deeper. The stack is a dependency chain. It is not a menu. Configuration layers (Chapter 2) come first. Nothing else is enforceable on a drifting fleet. You cannot gate workflows or trust hooks on machines you do not control.

Permissions and MCP distribution (Chapters 3 and 4) come next. They define the tool surface that every workflow will use.

Workflow gates and secrets governance (Chapters 5 and 6) sit on top of that surface. Speed is safe only when gates and data rules travel with it. Debugging (Chapter 7) and runbooks (Chapter 8) sit at the top. They assume the system below is instrumented and consistent. A runbook for a fleet you cannot reproduce is fiction. When a scenario asks what to fix first, climb from the bottom.

Next: Chapter 2, the foundation everything else assumes: rolling out Claude Code across the org with consistent configuration layers.

2. Rolling out Claude Code across an org: configuration layers

How to read this diagram
  1. Start at the top bar (Managed policy): set by IT, pushed to every machine, cannot be overridden.
  2. Move down to Project settings: checked into the repo, shared by the team.
  3. Then User settings: personal tweaks for one developer.
  4. Defaults at the bottom: out-of-box behavior.
  5. The arrow labeled "wins" is the lesson: when layers disagree, the higher one decides.

What breaks if a part fails: if you put a compliance rule in project settings, developers can edit it. An editable compliance rule is the same as no rule.

Why this comes next. Chapter 1 named the three drags: drift, unsafe speed, and invisible failures. The first fix is the least glamorous. It is also the most load-bearing. Make every developer's machine behave the same way. This chapter answers the question Chapter 1 left open.

How do you configure an agentic coding tool for 200 people? The organization's rules must be non-negotiable. Personal preference must still survive.

Rung 1: the one-paragraph version. Claude Code is Anthropic's agentic coding tool: it reads your repo, runs commands, edits files, and calls tools on your behalf. When one developer uses it, configuration is a personal preference. When 200 developers use it, configuration is governance.

Configuration layers are the stacked sources of settings. A higher layer overrides a lower one. The organization can set non-negotiable guardrails. Teams and individuals can still customize their own workflow. Without layers, you get three failures at once.

First, drift occurs. Every developer's install behaves differently. "It worked on my machine" becomes "it worked with my settings." Second, unenforceable policy occurs. Security's rules live in a file any developer can edit. They are suggestions. They are not controls.

Third, painful onboarding occurs. Each new hire hand-configures everything. They do not inherit the team's setup from the repository.

MANAGED policy (IT pushes, developer cannot override) -- compliance rules live here
   |
PROJECT settings (.claude/settings.json, checked into repo) -- team conventions
   |
USER settings (~/.claude/settings.json) -- personal defaults
   |
BUILT-IN defaults
   (permissions special rule: deny beats allow at any level)

Under the hood: the four layers

Rung 2: one level deeper. Settings resolve from the most specific authority down to defaults. From highest to lowest precedence:

  1. Managed (enterprise) policy. Set by IT or platform admins, pushed to every machine (for example, via device management). The developer cannot override this layer. This is where compliance rules live: allowed models, data-handling policy, hard deny rules.
  2. Project settings (.claude/settings.json in the repository). These settings are checked into version control. Everyone who clones the repository inherits the team's setup. This includes shared permissions, shared hooks, and project conventions. A personal settings.local.json file sits alongside it. This file holds per-developer tweaks. It is gitignored.
  3. User settings (~/.claude/settings.json). Personal defaults that follow the developer across every repo.
  4. Built-in defaults. What the tool does when nobody configured anything.

Context files follow a parallel idea. CLAUDE.md files give the agent persistent instructions. They exist at four scopes. An enterprise-level file comes from administrators. A project-level file is in the repository. This file contains team conventions and architecture notes. A user-level file contains personal preferences. A local per-project file (CLAUDE.local.md) is gitignored. It contains personal overrides. The agent loads the applicable files together. Repository knowledge travels with the repository. It does not live in one person's head.

Merge subtlety that the exam loves

For most settings, a more specific layer replaces a less specific one. But permissions merge with deny winning: if project settings deny a destructive command and the user's personal settings allow it, the deny still holds. And nothing in any lower layer can touch managed policy. Two consequences: a developer's local edits cannot weaken org guardrails, and a repo's checked-in settings protect every contributor automatically.

Worked example (illustrative numbers). Rung 3: the full climb. A 200-engineer fintech rolls out Claude Code. The platform team ships managed policy with 12 deny rules (no rm -rf, no sudo, no pushing to main without review tooling, no network calls to non-allowlisted hosts). Each repo gets a checked-in .claude/settings.json with the team's test commands and a project CLAUDE.md describing the service architecture.

Onboarding drops from about 2 hours of manual setup per developer. It drops to roughly 15 minutes. This includes install, sign in, and clone. One developer tries to allow sudo npm install in their personal settings. They want to "move faster." The managed deny rule still blocks it. The system logs the attempt.

How they will ask this

Scenario shape: "A healthcare company rolls out Claude Code to 150 engineers. Compliance requires that no developer can enable a model the security team has not approved, even by editing local files." Select one. The trap: An answer like "add the approved model list to each repo's .claude/settings.json" looks team-friendly. However, it is locally editable. So, it fails the "even by editing local files" constraint.

The credited answer pins the model allowlist in managed (enterprise) policy, the only layer a developer cannot override. A second trap: "Project settings replace user settings, so the repo controls everything." Wrong in two ways. First, permissions merge with deny-first rather than replacing. Second, a developer can edit the repo's settings file locally, so project-level rules are team convention, not org enforcement. Only the managed layer is truly non-overridable.

If the scenario mentions compliance, regulators, or "even if a developer changes their own settings," the answer lives in the managed layer. Exam relevance: D7 asks who controls what during a rollout. Read every scenario for the constraint. Compliance or "cannot be overridden" points to managed policy. Team consistency points to checked-in project settings. Personal preference points to user settings.

How to read this diagram
  1. Start at the top bar (Org policy): this is the managed layer. It is the widest bar because it covers every developer and every repo. Nothing below it can override it.
  2. Move down to Project settings: checked into the repo, shared by the team. It customizes workflow inside the boundaries the org set.
  3. Then User settings: personal tweaks for one developer across all repos.
  4. Defaults at the bottom: the tool's out-of-box behavior when nobody configured a value.
  5. The arrow on the right labeled "wins" is the whole lesson: when two layers disagree, the higher one decides. For permissions specifically, remember the extra rule: deny beats allow at any level.

What breaks if a layer fails: if the managed layer is missing, policy is unenforceable and every developer is a free agent. If project settings are missing, every repo is configured by tribal knowledge and onboarding is slow. If you confuse the layers, you will put a compliance rule in a file developers can edit, which is the same as having no rule.

Next: Chapter 3. Configuration decides what settings developers get. Permissions decide what the agent can do with them.

3. Permissions and guardrails: allow, ask, deny, plus hooks

How to read this diagram
  1. ALLOW: safe routine calls - read files, run tests. No friction.
  2. ASK: needs human approval - write production code, spend money.
  3. DENY: never permitted - exfiltrate secrets, disable guardrails.
  4. Hooks: the extra gate. PreToolUse scans the call BEFORE it runs.
  5. Remember: deny beats allow at any level.

What breaks if a part fails: if deny rules are missing, dangerous calls have no backstop and the ladder is decoration.

Why this comes next. Configuration layers (Chapter 2) decide what settings every developer gets. They do not decide what the agent can do with them. An agentic tool reads repositories. It runs commands. It edits files.

It has a blast radius. This chapter answers the question Chapter 2 left hanging. For each attempted action, who decides allow, ask, or deny?

How to read this diagram
  1. Every tool call is pattern-matched against the merged rules. It runs after this match. The first matching rule decides.
  2. ALLOW is for safe, known calls like a test suite: they run without prompting.
  3. ASK is the human gate: the agent pauses and waits for approval before a call with side effects.
  4. DENY blocks the call and logs it. When layers conflict, deny wins: the strongest guarantee beats the weaker ones.

What breaks if a part fails: If everything is ask, developers approve blindly and the gate becomes theater. If deny rules are missing, dangerous calls have no backstop.

Rung 1: the one-paragraph version. Claude Code is an agent. It takes actions in the real world. It runs shell commands. It edits files. It fetches URLs. The permission system decides for each attempted action. It decides if it runs silently. It decides if it pauses for human approval. It decides if it is blocked outright. There are three outcomes: allow (run without asking), ask (prompt the developer first), deny (block and log).

An agent with no permission model has an unlimited blast radius. This is the amount of damage one bad action can do. The model might run git push --force on the wrong branch. It might curl a malicious URL from a compromised dependency's README. It might delete a directory it misread.

Permissions shrink the blast radius. They shrink it to what the organization has explicitly accepted.

tool call --> [ rule match: first match wins, deny beats allow ] --> ALLOW (silent)
                                                                --> ASK (human approves)
                                                                --> DENY (blocked + logged)
                    ^--- PreToolUse hook gets a veto before execution

Under the hood

Rung 2: one level deeper. Every tool call is pattern-matched against the merged permission rules. This happens before it executes. Rules look like Bash(npm run test:*) (allow). They look like Bash(sudo *) (deny). They also look like WebFetch (ask). The first matching rule decides. On conflict between layers, deny wins.

Hooks are the programmatic enforcement point. A hook is a shell command the tool runs automatically at a lifecycle moment. First, PreToolUse fires right before a tool runs (it can block or modify the tool call). Next, PostToolUse fires after (for logging or validation). Then Stop fires when the agent finishes (for cleanup or checks). Session events like SessionStart are hooks too.

The classic enterprise pattern is a PreToolUse hook. This hook scans every Bash command. It scans against a denylist. A denylist is a list of blocked patterns. It also scans against a secret pattern. It blocks the command before the model ever sees the result. Hooks run with the developer's own shell privileges. Hook definitions themselves must be managed. They must be managed at the project or managed layer in high-trust environments. A user-editable hook is a hole. It is not a control.

{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": ["Bash(npm run test:*)", "Bash(git status)", "Read(//repo/src/**)"],
    "ask":   ["Bash(git push *)", "WebFetch"],
    "deny":  ["Bash(sudo *)", "Bash(rm -rf *)", "Bash(curl *)"]
  },
  "hooks": {
    "PreToolUse": [
      {"matcher": "Bash", "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "/opt/guardrails/scan-command.sh"}]}
    ]
  }
}

Reading the example: Tests and reads run freely. Pushes and web fetches pause for approval. Anything with sudo, recursive delete, or curl is hard-blocked. Before every Bash call, scan-command.sh gets the final say. It can veto.

Worked example (illustrative). Rung 3: the full climb. A platform team audits one quarter of agent sessions. About 12% triggered at least one "ask" prompt. Post-rollout surveys showed developers approved 97% of asks within seconds. After that finding, the team moved the genuinely dangerous patterns.

These included destructive git operations and package publishes. They moved them from ask to deny at the managed layer. Destructive-command incidents fell to zero the next quarter. "Ask" volume dropped by half. Asks were reserved for real judgment calls.

How they will ask this

Scenario shape: "After a rollout, an agent ran git push --force and overwrote a release branch. The team had set push commands to 'ask.' What control would have prevented this?" Select one. The trap: "require ask for all Bash commands" or "train developers to read prompts carefully." Both keep the human as the safety mechanism. Humans under deadline click through.

The credited answer is a deny rule on destructive git patterns at the managed layer, which removes the human from the critical path entirely. "Ask is a safety control" is the deeper confusion: ask is a speed bump, not a control. Developers under deadline click through prompts (prompt fatigue), so ask only slows accidents; it does not prevent them.

Deny is the only hard control. The exam exploits this: whenever the scenario demands a guarantee ("must never," "compliance requires"), ask is the trap and deny is the answer. Exam relevance: D7 frames permissions as the blast-radius control for agentic tools. Expect trade-off questions: velocity (allow) versus safety (deny), and where enforcement must live (managed layer) to survive local edits.

How to read this diagram
  1. Start at the left card "Tool call": the agent wants to run something, for example a Bash command.
  2. Follow the arrow to the blue diamond "Rule match". The tool call is pattern-matched against the merged allow/ask/deny rules. The first match wins. Deny beats allow.
  3. There are three exits. Up to "Allow" (green check) means it runs silently. Right to "Ask" (amber) pauses for the small "Human approves" step. Down to "Deny" (red X) blocks it outright. It logs the attempt.
  4. The "Hook runs" card at the bottom feeds into the decision from below: a PreToolUse hook gets a veto before execution, even over an allow.
  5. Read the teaching point off the colors: green is convenience, amber is friction, red is the only guarantee.

What breaks if a part fails: If rules are too loose, the agent's blast radius is unbounded. If everything is "ask," developers develop click-through reflexes. The friction buys nothing. If hooks are user-editable, the person it is supposed to restrain can remove the veto.

Next: Chapter 4. Permissions cover actions; now the tools themselves: distributing MCP servers to every team safely.

4. Distributing MCP servers to teams

How to read this diagram
  1. Vet: security review of the server before anyone installs it.
  2. Package: versioned bundle with docs, so installs are repeatable.
  3. Distribute: managed install to every machine - no hand-wiring.
  4. Update: rotate credentials, patch, deprecate old versions.
  5. The bottom panel is the auth rule: per-user OAuth, never shared service-account passwords.

What breaks if a part fails: if servers are hand-wired per developer, you get ad-hoc sprawl: unvetted servers with shared credentials.

Why this comes next. Permissions and guardrails (Chapter 3) control what the agent may do. They say nothing about where the agent's tools come from. This chapter answers the distribution question Chapter 3 left open: who vets MCP servers, which teams get them, and whose credentials they use.

How to read this diagram
  1. PROJECT scope lives in .mcp.json at the repo root, checked in: the whole team gets the same tools.
  2. LOCAL scope is the default: this project only, your agent, your checkout.
  3. USER scope lives in your Claude Code config: all your projects.
  4. The vetted registry feeds project scope: teams inherit approved servers instead of inventing their own.

What breaks if a part fails: If team behavior lives in user scope, every developer is a free agent. If secrets land in the checked-in file, the repo becomes a credential leak.

Rung 1: the one-paragraph version. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the open standard that connects Claude to external tools and data through MCP servers: small services that expose tools (for example, "search the docs," "read a ticket," "check CI status" (CI, continuous integration: the automated build-and-test pipeline)).

Distributing MCP servers means you decide which servers every developer gets. You decide who vets the servers. You decide whose credentials the servers use. You do not let each developer hand-wire their own servers. Ad-hoc MCP sprawl is a quiet disaster. One developer adds an unvetted server with write access to the production database.

Another developer pastes a personal API key into a config file. The system commits this file.

Nobody can answer "which tools can our agents touch right now," and when a contractor leaves, nobody knows which keys to rotate. Central distribution turns the tool surface into an inventory: known servers, known scopes, one place to revoke.

[VETTED REGISTRY] --> Team A/B/C/D (shared checked-in .mcp.json)
        |                  |
   (review gate)      scoped per-user OAuth auth + secrets in a vault
        |
  every new server expands 3 things: capability + attack surface + token cost

Under the hood

Rung 2: one level deeper. MCP server configurations live in .mcp.json files at project scope (at the repo root, checked into the repo, shared by the team). They also live in the user's Claude Code config: at local scope (this project only, the default) and user scope (all projects). The org pattern has three parts:

  1. A vetted registry. A central catalog of approved MCP servers. Each entry records what the server can do, what data it touches, and its risk tier. Adding a server is a review decision, like adding a dependency.
  2. Shared project configs. Teams get the vetted servers through a checked-in .mcp.json, so every developer's agent sees the same tool surface on day one.
  3. Per-user, least-privilege auth. Remote MCP servers authenticate with OAuth 2.0. This is the industry standard for delegated sign-in. The developer logs in one time. The server receives a narrowly scoped token. This token replaces a shared password or API key. Each developer signs in as themselves. They use narrowly scoped permissions. For example, they have read-only issue tracker access. They do not share one static API key baked into a file. When someone leaves, you revoke their grant. Nobody else is affected.

There is a deeper reason architects care. Every MCP server you add expands three things at once: the agent's capabilities (what it can do), the attack surface (what a compromised or malicious server can do), and the token cost (tool definitions consume context on every request). This is the D3 "capability bloat" idea applied to developer tooling: the tool list is an architecture decision, not plumbing.

Worked example (illustrative). Rung 3: the full climb. A 60-person organization vets three MCP servers. These servers are docs search (read-only), issue tracker (read-only), and CI status (read-only). A team requests a fourth server. This server is a database admin server with write access.

The team wants this server "to speed up debugging." Registry review rejects write access. It approves a read-only variant. Two months later, that server's upstream dependency is compromised. Access was read-only and per-user OAuth. Because of this, the blast radius is contained to reads. The security team revokes the server from the registry in one place.

They do not hunt through 60 personal configs.

How they will ask this

Scenario shape: "A team shares a .mcp.json containing a database MCP server configured with a single shared API key committed in the file. A contractor with repo access leaves the company." Select two. The trap: "rotate the shared key immediately" is only half the fix; it treats the symptom.

The credited pair identifies the design flaw (shared static credential with no per-user identity, committed in version control) and the structural fix (per-user OAuth with least-privilege scopes, secrets in a vault, server vetted through the registry). Rotating the key without changing the pattern guarantees a repeat. The deeper trap: "MCP config is just developer convenience." On this exam, the MCP tool list is a security and cost surface.

A scenario mentions unvetted servers. It mentions shared static keys. It mentions "agents can suddenly do more than expected." This scenario tests if you centralize distribution with scoped auth. It does not test if developers find the config convenient. Exam relevance: D7 tests the distribution mechanism against a constraint. "Revocable centrally" or "contractor leaves" points to per-user OAuth through a managed registry. "Consistent tool surface" points to checked-in project .mcp.json.

As you learned in D3, an MCP server is the reuse mechanism when one capability must serve many surfaces. This volume is about distributing those servers safely.

How to read this diagram
  1. Start at the center: the Registry (blue, with a gear). This is the vetted catalog. Nothing reaches a developer's agent without passing through it.
  2. Follow the four arrows outward to Team A through D: each team receives the same approved server list via a shared, checked-in config. Consistency is the point.
  3. Each team card connects to a small key icon ("Scoped auth"): credentials are per-team or per-user OAuth grants with narrow scopes, not one shared key.
  4. The arrow down to the vault ("Secrets"): actual secret values live in a secrets manager, never in the config files developers see.

What breaks if a part fails: no registry means unvetted servers with unknown scopes. Shared static keys mean one leak or one departure forces a painful global rotation. Secrets in config files mean the credential is one accidental commit away from exposure.

Next: Chapter 5. The fleet is configured, guarded, and tooled. Now, the workflow: where AI helps and where humans gate.

5. AI-assisted development workflows: where AI helps, where humans gate

How to read this diagram
  1. Draft (AI): generate code, tests, docs. Fast, fluent, possibly wrong.
  2. Verify (deterministic): compiler, type checker, test suite. No judgment needed.
  3. Gate (human): review the diff, check the spec, approve. Judgment lives here.
  4. The red panel names the trap: "The AI wrote tests, so the change is tested." Ask instead: do the tests assert the specified behavior? Who verified the spec?

What breaks if a part fails: if the review gate is skipped, wrong-but-confident code ships; if tests are skipped, you have decoration, not verification.

Why this comes next. Chapters 2 through 4 built a governed fleet: consistent config, permission guardrails, vetted tools. But a governed fleet with no designed workflow still lets AI output flow straight to production. This chapter answers the workflow question: which tasks AI may do freely, and which gates every AI-produced change must pass before it ships.

How to read this diagram
  1. GREEN is AI-friendly: boilerplate, test scaffolding, docstrings, explaining legacy code. Light review.
  2. YELLOW means review carefully: new business logic, shared-code refactors, dependency changes. Read for behavior at the boundaries, not style.
  3. RED is the senior gate: auth, cryptography, DB migrations, irreversible actions. Senior review plus passing tests, no exceptions.
  4. The tier picks the gate. Risk rises top to bottom, so gate strength must rise with it.

What breaks if a part fails: If red-tier work gets green-tier review, defects ship at machine speed. If everything is red-tier, the team drowns in review queues.

Rung 1: the one-paragraph version. AI-assisted development means AI tools participate in the normal development loop. They draft code. They generate tests. They explain legacy code. They refactor code.

They write documents. The architect's job is not to "allow AI" or "ban AI." It is to design the workflow. This workflow defines which tasks the AI may do freely. It defines which gates every AI-produced change must pass before it ships.

AI output is fluent and confident. This makes its failure modes sneaky. It can hallucinate APIs that look real. It can create insecure patterns, such as string-concatenated SQL. It can use outdated library usage. It can have subtly wrong business logic.

Without gates, you do not get faster engineering. You get defects at machine speed. The workflow converts raw generation into reliable throughput.

GREEN (AI-friendly): boilerplate, test scaffolding, docstrings, small refactors --> light review
YELLOW (review carefully): new business logic, shared code, deps --> behavior review
RED (senior gate): auth, crypto, migrations, irreversible --> senior review + tests, no exceptions

Under the hood: draft with AI, verify with determinism

Rung 2: one level deeper. The pattern that works is a split of responsibilities. The AI drafts; deterministic systems and humans verify. Concretely:

  • Green tier (AI-friendly): boilerplate, test scaffolding from a spec, docstrings, explaining unfamiliar code, small refactors with full test coverage. Light review.
  • Yellow tier (review carefully): new business logic, refactors touching shared code, dependency changes. The reviewer reads for behavior, not style: does it do the right thing at the boundaries?
  • Red tier (senior gate): authentication, cryptography, database migrations, anything irreversible or security-sensitive. Requires senior review and passing tests, no exceptions.

Verification is layered. The compiler and type checker catch syntax and type errors. Linters catch style and known-bad patterns. The test suite catches behavior regressions. The human reviewer catches wrong requirements and wrong assumptions. No single layer is enough.

This is because each layer catches a different class of mistake.

Worked example (illustrative). Rung 3: the full climb. A team measures its first quarter with AI assistance. Pull requests merge about 30% faster. However, pull requests with no test changes show roughly double the revert rate of pull requests with tests. The team responds with a workflow rule.

This is not a ban. Every AI-generated change must include tests. Or, it must carry an explicit reviewer sign-off. This sign-off notes why tests were skipped. Revert rates converge back to baseline within a quarter. Velocity stays up.

How they will ask this

Scenario shape: "After adopting AI coding tools, a team's PR velocity doubles but production incidents rise. Investigation shows AI-generated PRs are being rubber-stamped. Which two changes best address this?" Select two. The trap: "ban AI tools for production code" (throws away the velocity) or "require longer review checklists" (checklists get skimmed).

The credited pair targets the failure mode. These are tiered review gates and behavior-level review standards. Red-tier changes need senior review plus tests. Reviewers verify what the code does at boundaries. Generated tests are checked against the specification. They are not just executed.

The deeper trap is a false belief: the AI wrote tests, so the change is tested. Generated tests can encode the same misunderstanding as the generated code. If the AI misread the requirement, its tests assert the wrong behavior and pass. Tests are only as good as the specification they encode. On review, the question is never the count of tests. Ask two questions instead: do the tests assert the specified behavior, and who verified the spec? Exam relevance: D7 asks you to design the workflow under a constraint.

Regulated industry or security-sensitive code points to mandatory human gates at the red tier. Velocity complaints point to keeping green-tier friction near zero, not to removing gates.

How to read this diagram
  1. Read the top lane ("AI drafts") left to right: Code → Tests → Docs. These are the generation tasks where AI adds the most speed. Blue arrows show the draft flowing forward.
  2. Follow the dashed arrows down from each draft card to the bottom lane ("Human gates"): every draft meets a gate. Code meets Review, tests meet Run tests (actually execute them, not just admire them), docs meet Approve.
  3. The amber check icons on the gates are the point: nothing flows to Ship without passing its gate. The final blue arrow to "Ship" only exists because the gates held.

What breaks if a part fails: If you skip the review gate, wrong-but-confident code ships. If you skip running the tests, you have decoration. You do not have verification. If you let AI output skip gates, you reintroduce the defect stream. This happens "because it is just a small change." The workflow was built to stop this defect stream.

Next: Chapter 6. Workflows gate what ships; now what may flow in: secrets and data governance for AI tooling.

6. Secrets and data governance in AI tooling

How to read this diagram
  1. POLICY: the written rule - what data classes may go to which tools. Customer PII and secrets go to no AI tool at all.
  2. PREVENTION: make the mistake hard. The PreToolUse hook blocks secret patterns BEFORE the model sees anything.
  3. DETECTION: catch what slipped through - redacted transcripts, secret scanning over repos and logs.
  4. RESPONSE: the rotation runbook - which credential, who owns it, how fast it rotates.
  5. The subtitle carries the worked result: the hook is also a teacher.

What breaks if a part fails: if prevention is missing, one pasted secret is a breach. If logs are not redacted, detection tooling finds the secret. Anyone with log access could also find it.

Why this comes next. Chapter 5 designed the gates for AI-produced code. Those gates assume the inputs were safe to use in the first place. This chapter answers the question Chapter 5 left open. What information is allowed to flow into AI tools? What must never cross the organization's boundary?

A prompt is data. This chapter treats it that way.

How to read this diagram
  1. MAY FLOW (with rules): public code anywhere, internal code only to tools under the org data agreement, anonymized tickets after PII redaction.
  2. Secrets cross by NAME, never by value: reference the DB_PASSWORD env var, never paste the value.
  3. MUST NEVER CROSS: API keys, passwords, private keys, tokens, customer PII, source code with no vendor data agreement.
  4. Anything under a never policy stays out. Where available, use zero-data-retention terms.

What breaks if a part fails: If prevention is missing, one pasted secret is a breach. A PreToolUse hook that blocks secret patterns before the model sees them is the backstop.

Rung 1: the one-paragraph version. Secrets and data governance answers one question. What information is allowed to flow into AI tools? What must never leave the organization's boundary? Secrets are credentials. These include API keys, passwords, private keys, and tokens.

Data governance covers the rest. This includes customer PII (personally identifiable information). It includes source code from restricted repositories. It includes internal documents.

A prompt is data, and data sent to a tool can end up in logs, vendor systems, or training pipelines depending on the provider's policy. Developers paste secrets into AI tools for the most sympathetic reason: they are debugging, and the secret is part of the broken context. One pasted production key is a full incident: rotate the credential, audit for misuse, explain it to security. Prevention is orders of magnitude cheaper than the incident.

POLICY (what may go where) --> PREVENTION (PreToolUse hook scans, reference by NAME not value)
                                    --> DETECTION (redacted logs + secret scanning)
                                            --> RESPONSE (rotation runbook)

Under the hood: four layers of defense

Rung 2: one level deeper. Four layers, in the order they act:

  1. Policy: This is a written rule. It states what data classes may go to which tools. For example, public code may go anywhere. Internal code may only go to tools under the organization's data agreement. Customer PII and secrets may not go to any AI tool. Where available, use zero-data-retention (ZDR) terms. This ensures the vendor does not retain prompts.
  2. Prevention: Make the mistake hard to commit. A PreToolUse hook scans prompts and tool inputs. It scans for secret patterns. These patterns include sk-..., AKIA..., and PEM private-key headers. It blocks the call before the model sees anything. Developers reference secrets by name. For example, they use "use the DB_PASSWORD env var." They never reference secrets by value. Sensitive paths are excluded from what the agent may read. This is like a .gitignore for the agent's eyes.
  3. Detection: Stored transcripts and logs are redacted. Secret-shaped strings are replaced before writing. Secret scanning runs over repositories and logs. This catches what slipped through.
  4. Response: This is a rotation runbook. It states which credential. It states who owns it. It states how fast it can be replaced. It states who gets notified.

Worked example (illustrative). Rung 3: the full climb. An org deploys the secret-scanning hook to all 200 developers. In the first month it blocks 34 paste attempts, most of them AWS-style keys pasted during debugging sessions. Each block shows the developer a message: "Blocked: this looks like a credential. Reference it by environment variable name instead." Paste attempts drop by 80% in the second month, because the hook is also a teacher.

How they will ask this

Scenario shape: "An engineer pastes a production database password into Claude Code while debugging a connection issue.

The organization's vendor agreement includes zero data retention." Select two. The trap: "no action needed, ZDR means the vendor retained nothing." The credited pair: rotate the credential immediately. Local transcripts, shell history, and logs are outside ZDR's scope. Then, add a PreToolUse hook. This hook blocks secret-shaped input before it reaches the model. This prevents the next tired engineer from repeating the mistake.

The deeper trap: "We have an enterprise agreement with zero data retention, so pasting secrets is fine." Two holes. First, ZDR covers the vendor's API, not your laptop: local transcripts, shell history, and your own logs may still hold the secret. Second, retention terms are about storage, not about the human and system exposure in between.

The rule stands regardless of contract. Reference secrets by name. Never reference them by value. A leaked credential gets rotated. This is true even if you believe nobody retained it. Exam relevance: D7 tests prevention over detection.

The scenario describes a leak vector. The credited control stops the data from leaving the boundary. This control is a hook or reference-by-name. It is not a control that finds the data afterward, such as scanning or audit.

How to read this diagram
  1. Read the left panel ("Risky") first: a chat bubble containing a masked secret (dots and stars) with a red X. This is the paste-the-value anti-pattern. The value has now entered a transcript, a log, and possibly a vendor system.
  2. Read the right panel ("Safe"): the chat bubble contains only a reference name. An arrow leads to a vault icon, which holds the actual value outside the conversation. A second arrow leads to "Redacted log": even the stored record carries no secret.
  3. The teaching point is the direction of the arrows: the secret value never enters the prompt, the transcript, or the log. Only the name travels.

What breaks if a part fails: if the hook is missing, prevention depends on human discipline at 2am, which is no prevention at all. If logs are not redacted, detection tooling finds the secret but so could anyone with log access. If there is no rotation runbook, a leak becomes a week-long incident instead of a one-hour one.

Next: Chapter 7. Data rules are set; now forensics: debugging production Claude systems from their traces.

7. Debugging production Claude systems: trace forensics

How to read this diagram
  1. Correlation ID: tie every span to one run. Without it you debug a different incident.
  2. Stop reasons: learn why the model stopped, not just that it stopped.
  3. Tool pairs: inspect tool_use / tool_result pairs. Most production bugs live here.
  4. Frozen replay: re-run the exact inputs - same model, same prompt, same tool versions.
  5. The bottom panel: the credited answer checks tool definitions and their recent change history first.

What breaks if a part fails: if you change the model version mid-debug, you debug a different incident. Frozen replay is what makes the trace trustworthy.

Why this comes next. Chapters 2 through 6 built the governed fleet. This includes config, permissions, tools, workflows, and data rules. This chapter starts from the day all of that exists. Something still misbehaves. It answers the forensics question the earlier chapters never could.

You have only traces and no debugger. How do you figure out why the agent did the wrong thing?

How to read this diagram
  1. The exact inputs: model version, temperature, system prompt. Without these you cannot replay.
  2. The capability surface: the tool schemas the model could call.
  3. Every tool_use / tool_result pair: where most production bugs live.
  4. Stop reason first: max_tokens is a budget problem; tool_use versus end_turn tells you whether the model acted or answered.
  5. Token usage per stage: the cost ledger.

What breaks if a part fails: If the correlation ID does not flow through your stack, one user complaint maps to nothing. If tool results are not logged, the most common bug class is invisible.

Rung 1: the one-paragraph version. Debugging a production Claude system means finding why the agent did the wrong thing. The agent may use the wrong tool. It may use the wrong arguments. It may enter a loop. It may give a confident but false answer. You cannot attach a debugger to a conversation. You debug with traces. A trace is the complete record of a request. A trace holds the system prompt. It holds every message. It holds every tool_use block with its exact input.

It holds every tool_result and the stop_reason of each step (why the model stopped: tool_use, end_turn, max_tokens). It holds token counts, latencies, and a correlation ID tying it all to one user session. LLM failures are non-deterministic and stateful: the same prompt can produce different behavior on different runs, and each step depends on everything before it. Without traces you are left with "it worked when I tried it," which resolves nothing.

The trace is the core dump of an agentic system.

request --> tool call --> tool result --> tool call --> tool result --> answer
   \________________ correlation ID ties it all together ________________/
debug order: stop reasons first --> tool_use/tool_result pairs --> schema history
              --> frozen replay with canned results --> binary-search the trace

Under the hood: the forensics workflow

Rung 2: one level deeper. Five steps, always in this order:

  1. Capture everything, keyed by correlation ID. Log the full request/response cycle: model version, temperature, system prompt, tool schemas, every tool input and result. The correlation ID must flow through your stack so one user complaint maps to one trace.
  2. Read the stop reasons first. max_tokens means "the model was cut off mid-thought." This is a budget problem. It is not a reasoning problem. tool_use versus end_turn shows if the model chose to act or chose to answer.
  3. Inspect the tool_use / tool_result pairs. Most production bugs are here. The model passed the wrong argument. The tool returned something unexpected. The model coped badly. Check the tool schemas too. A schema may change. For example, a field name may change. A type may change from string to number. The model may call a contract that does not exist. Schema drift is a common problem.
  4. Reproduce with frozen inputs. Re-running the prompt is not reproduction: temperature above zero and live tool results make every run diverge. True reproduction means replaying the trace with identical inputs: same model version, same system prompt, and canned tool results recorded from the failing run. If the replay diverges, the nondeterminism itself is a clue.
  5. Binary-search the trace. Replay up to tool call N with canned results. See where behavior first goes wrong. The fault is between the last good step and the first bad step.

Worked example (illustrative). Rung 3: the full climb. A support ticket says: "the assistant booked the wrong hotel dates." The trace has 14 tool calls. It has approximately 38k input tokens. It shows the fault at call 9. The hotel search tool returned dates in DD/MM/YYYY. This happened after a vendor update. The agent's instructions assumed MM/DD/YYYY. The model did not misbehave. It used a mislabeled input. Fix this by normalizing dates in the tool wrapper. This is deterministic code. Do not tweak the prompt. The forensics took 20 minutes. This is because the trace was complete. Without it, the team would spend days prompt-tuning a data bug.

How they will ask this

Scenario shape: "An agent intermittently calls the wrong tool. The prompts in the failing traces are identical to the prompts in successful traces." Select one. The trap: "lower the temperature" or "rewrite the system prompt." Identical prompts producing different behavior means the non-prompt inputs changed.

The credited answer checks two things before touching the prompt at all. First, the tool definitions and their recent change history (schema drift: a renamed field, a changed description, a newly added overlapping tool). Second, the contents of the tool results. The deeper trap: "Re-running the prompt reproduces the bug." It does not, unless you freeze everything the run depended on. Temperature, model version, the system prompt, the tool schemas, and every tool result are all inputs.

If you change any of them, you debug a different incident. Frozen replay with canned tool results is the standard for "reproduced." Exam relevance: D7's "support debugging" objective is diagnostic reasoning. You get a symptom. The credited move is the artifact that finds the fault fastest. Use stop reasons for cut-off behavior. Use tool_use/tool_result pairs for wrong actions.

Use schema history for intermittent wrong-tool calls.

How to read this diagram
  1. Read the top row left to right. This shows: Request → Tool call → Tool result → Tool call → Tool result → Answer. These are the trace nodes. Each node is logged with its exact inputs and outputs. They are under one correlation ID.
  2. The magnifier over "Frozen inputs" is the method: when a failure occurs, you freeze everything (model version, prompts, schemas, tool results) instead of re-running live.
  3. The amber "Replay" arrow loops from the end back to the start. It shows the debug cycle. Feed the frozen trace back through the system. Watch where behavior first differs from the recording.
  4. The caption's one-line lesson: replay the recorded trace with identical inputs, or you are not debugging the incident you think you are.

What breaks if a part fails: no correlation ID and you cannot find the trace for a complaint. No logged tool results and you cannot freeze the replay. No schema versioning and schema drift becomes invisible. Re-running live instead of replaying and the bug "disappears," which teaches you nothing.

Next: Chapter 8. Forensics explains the past; now readiness for the future: operational runbooks for LLM apps.

8. Operational runbooks for LLM apps

How to read this diagram
  1. DETECT: the spend dashboard spikes to 40x baseline; alerts fire on 300+ tool-call sessions.
  2. TRIAGE: which sessions, which tool, what is the blast radius?
  3. MITIGATE: kill sessions via the admin API, flip on the iteration cap. Stop the bleeding.
  4. ROOT-CAUSE: read the traces - the tool always returned retry, and the agent obeyed forever.
  5. HARDEN: terminal error after 3 retries; fix the wrapper.
  6. The order is the lesson: every minute of diagnosis is money burning while the loop still runs.

What breaks if a part fails: if you diagnose before mitigating, the runaway loop keeps spending while you read traces.

Why this comes next. Chapter 7 taught trace forensics. This is how to reconstruct what the agent did after a failure. Forensics is reactive. This chapter answers the proactive question Chapter 7 left open. What is the written procedure the on-call engineer follows at 3am?

This is for failure modes that traditional runbooks never imagined.

How to read this diagram
  1. Runaway agentic loops: the agent calls tools forever. Kill switch: disable the agent endpoint.
  2. Cost spikes: a loop burns money while the app looks healthy. Alert on spend per hour, not just uptime.
  3. Prompt-injection success: a tool result smuggles instructions in. Treat tool output as untrusted input.
  4. Context-window overflow: the conversation outgrows the model's memory, so outputs get truncated. Fail gracefully with a summary prompt, and keep a compaction strategy ready.
  5. Behavior drift after a model upgrade: answers change even though your code did not. Trend eval scores across the upgrade, roll back to the pinned version, and gate every future upgrade on evals.

What breaks if a part fails: If you only alert when the app is down, a cost spike can burn money for hours. Everything may look healthy.

Rung 1: the one-paragraph version. A runbook is the written procedure the on-call engineer follows when something breaks: symptoms, what to check, what to do, in what order. LLM apps need runbooks for failure modes traditional runbooks never imagined.

There are five types of failures: runaway agentic loops, cost spikes, prompt-injection attempts, context-window overflow, and behavior drift. A runaway agentic loop means the agent calls tools forever. A cost spike means a loop burns money. Prompt-injection attempts are hostile instructions. They are smuggled in through tool output or documents. The model mistakes them for commands.

Context-window overflow means the conversation outgrows the model's memory. Behavior drift means the model's answers change after the vendor updates the model. This occurs even if your code does not change. This happens after a model version change.

At 3am nobody reasons from first principles. The runbook converts judgment into a checklist, so the response is fast and consistent no matter who is on call. It also encodes the lesson of every previous incident, so the org only pays for each failure mode once.

DETECT (leading indicators) --> TRIAGE (blast radius) --> MITIGATE (kill switch first)
        --> ROOT CAUSE (trace forensics) --> HARDEN (guardrail so it cannot recur)

Under the hood: the incident loop

Rung 2: one level deeper. Every LLM runbook page follows the same four phases:

  1. Detect. Alerts on leading indicators, not just outages: tool calls per session, tokens per session, spend per hour, error rate on tool calls, injection-pattern matches. If you only alert on "the app is down," a cost spike can burn money for hours while the app looks healthy.
  2. Triage. Scope the blast radius: how many sessions, which users, since when, which model version and prompt version. Grab the correlation IDs; you will need the traces later.
  3. Mitigate.
  4. Mitigate. Stop the bleeding before diagnosing. The kill switches are: disable the agent endpoint. Revoke the API key. Flip the feature flag. A feature flag is a remote on/off switch for a feature. You flip it without redeploying. Cap the maximum tool iterations per session. Enforce a per-session spend limit. Mitigation buys time. It is not the fix.
  5. Root cause and harden.
  6. Root cause and harden. Now do the trace forensics from Section 7. Every incident must end with a hardening item. This is a guardrail, a cap, a validation, or a test. It makes this class of incident impossible or self-limiting. An incident with no hardening item will recur.

The guardrails that make runbooks work are built before the incident. These include per-request timeouts, maximum iterations per agent session, spend alerts with automatic caps, and circuit breakers on failing tools. A circuit breaker stops calling a failing service for a while. This prevents retries from adding to an outage. A runbook without these is a checklist with no levers.

Incident Leading signal First action (mitigate) Hardening
Runaway agentic loop Tool calls/session far above baseline Kill the sessions, cap max iterations Idempotent tools, max-retry in wrappers
Cost spike Spend/hour alert Per-session spend cap, disable endpoint if needed Budget alerts with auto-throttle
Prompt injection attempt Injection-pattern match in inputs Block the session, preserve the trace Input validation, least-privilege tools
Context overflow Token counts near the limit, truncated outputs Fail gracefully with a summary prompt Compaction strategy, shorter tool results
Behavior drift (new model version) Eval scores or task success drop after deploy Roll back to the pinned version Pin versions, eval gate on every upgrade

Worked example (illustrative). Rung 3: the full climb. At 2am the spend dashboard spikes to 40x baseline. Alert: sessions average 300+ tool calls. On-call follows the runbook. They kill the affected sessions via the admin API.

They flip on the 25-iteration cap. Mitigation takes 8 minutes. Traces show a tool that always returned "retry." The agent obeyed forever. The team fixed the root cause the next day: the tool wrapper now returns a terminal error after 3 retries.

Hardening: the iteration cap and a per-session spend limit of $5 stay on permanently. Total burn: about $180 over 20 minutes. Without the runbook's kill switch, the loop would have run until morning standup.

How they will ask this

Scenario shape: At 2am the spend dashboard spikes 40x. Agent sessions show 300+ tool calls each. Two candidate first actions are: (a) read the traces to find the bug, (b) kill the sessions and enforce an iteration cap, then investigate. Select one, with justification. The trap: (a) feels diligent. The engineer wants to understand before acting. But every minute of diagnosis burns money. The loop is still running.

The credited answer is (b): stop the bleed first, then diagnose. A follow-up item will then ask for the hardening change. This includes iteration caps, idempotent tools, and spend limits. An idempotent tool is safe to retry. Running the tool twice has the same effect as running it once. This is where the lasting fix lives. The deeper trap is: "The runbook is the fix." The runbook buys time. Mitigation stops the damage. The fix is the code change. Prevention is the hardening item.

Teams that stop at mitigation collect the same incident every quarter. The exam will offer "follow the runbook's mitigation steps" as a distractor when the question asks for the lasting fix, and vice versa. Exam relevance: D7's "operational issue resolution" maps directly to this loop. The exam rewards mitigate-before-diagnose ordering and kill-switch selection matched to the failure mode.

How to read this diagram
  1. Read the four cards left to right: Detect (bell icon: the alert fires on a leading indicator), Triage (list icon: scope the blast radius), Mitigate (shield icon: the kill switch), Root cause (wrench icon: trace forensics).
  3. The small caption under each card is its job. For example, "alert fires," "scope blast radius," "kill switch," "trace forensics." If you do forensics before the kill switch, you read the diagram backwards.
  5. The dashed amber "harden" arrow curves from Root cause back to Detect. This is the most important line in the figure. Every incident must produce a guardrail. This guardrail feeds back into detection and prevention.

What breaks if a part fails: no leading-indicator alerts and you detect cost spikes from the invoice. No kill switch and mitigation is a code deploy during an incident. No hardening loop and the runbook becomes a museum of recurring incidents.

Next: the Exam-day notes for D7, which compress this whole volume into the shapes the exam will actually ask.

Exam-day notes for D7

How to read this diagram
  1. How they ask it: production scenarios with a constraint. Do not memorize config paths.
  2. "Most correct" distractors: several options partly right. Ask which GUARANTEES the outcome. Deny beats ask.
  3. Rollout order: managed policy first, then project conventions, then personal settings.
  4. Incident order: detect, triage, mitigate, root-cause, harden.
  5. Debug order: correlation ID, stop reasons, tool pairs, frozen replay.

What breaks if a part fails: if you memorize paths instead of orders, the scenario items will punish you - the exam tests precedence, not trivia.

How to spend your study time on the smallest domain
  • Four questions, scenario-shaped. D7 is 7% of the exam, roughly 4 of 63 items. Each one is a production scenario with a constraint. Do not memorize config file paths; practice constraint-first reading: find the constraint in the scenario ("even if a developer edits local files," "must never," "at 2am"), then pick the control that satisfies it.
  • "Most correct" distractors are the norm. Several options will be partially right. Ask which option guarantees the outcome under the stated constraint: deny beats ask, prevention beats detection, mitigation beats diagnosis, managed layer beats project settings.
  • Know the order of operations. Rollout: managed policy first, then project conventions, then personal settings. Incident: detect, triage, mitigate, root-cause, harden. Debug: correlation ID, stop reasons, tool pairs, frozen replay. If an answer choice violates the order, it is wrong.
  • Watch for the human-weakness traps. "Ask the developer to approve" fails under deadline pressure. "Review the prompt" fails when inputs changed. "Rely on the vendor agreement" fails for local data. The exam keeps testing whether you design for how systems actually fail, not how they should behave.
A fair question: do I need hands-on Claude Code experience for these questions?

It helps, but the questions are for the architect level. This includes rollout design, policy layering, workflow gates, and incident response. If you understand the four configuration layers, you can answer every D7 scenario. You must understand the allow/ask/deny trade-off. You must understand the draft-and-gate workflow. You must understand frozen-replay debugging.

You must understand the mitigate-before-diagnose runbook loop. This volume alone provides this information. The exam explicitly tests design decisions and trade-offs. It does not test configuration trivia.

How to read this diagram
  1. Permissions: deny beats ask. A must-never rule is not satisfied by a pause.
  2. Secrets: prevention beats detection. Block before the model sees, do not scan after.
  3. Incidents: mitigation beats diagnosis. Stop the bleeding before naming the cause.
  4. Rollout: managed layer beats project settings. Know the order of operations cold: managed first, then permissions, then tools, then data rules.

What breaks if a part fails:

What breaks if a part fails: The classic D7 trap is the most correct distractor. This is an option that helps. But it does not guarantee the outcome under the stated constraint.
